# Publish, with fewer decisions at once

**Notebook → GitHub repository → website host.** Connecting saves the source. Publishing creates a viewing copy.

Select a numbered state to discuss it. Interact with its buttons to try the flow; use ↻ in its footer to reset. These are editable components, not screenshots. **No real publishing occurs.**

## What changes

**One decision per stage.** Repository setup comes first; hosting follows. Completed setup collapses into a small summary.

**Defaults do the work.** Derive the repository name from the notebook. Keep branch selection in Advanced. Use one primary action.

**Two distinct statuses.** Git can be connected or updated while the website is still unpublished or deploying. Never call that “live.”

**Keep visibility explicit.** Public source is a separate disclosure from a public website. Private-source hosting depends on provider eligibility.

**Repeat publishing is the main screen.** Show the URL, last published version and changes. Don’t bring the setup form back.

**Recover the failed step.** A deployment failure shouldn’t send the user back through repository creation.

## Questions to resolve

1. **Does Git belong here?** Publish can guide first-time connection, but Git settings may deserve their own home once connected.

2. **What is shared?** This concept publishes the whole viewing notebook. If page-level publishing is required, scope selection needs a real model, not a hidden dropdown.

3. **When does Git update?** Here, Publish saves the version to GitHub and deploys it. Continuous Git sync would need its own status and conflict behavior.

4. **How do external hosts deploy?** Vercel/Netlify may deploy on push. We must reconcile that with an explicit Publish button before promising both behaviors.

5. **Existing repositories need a check.** The concept includes a check step; it must handle incompatible contents and permissions before connection.

## Grounded in Design Notebook

The folder is the work. The app is a viewer and editor. A published site is a portable viewing copy.

The ninth state explores additional hosts. **It does not claim Vercel or Netlify integration exists today.**

[Design Notebook ethos](https://github.com/dfosco/design-notebook)

# Publish flows

Each panel is a separate component widget. Follow arrows left to right. Failure states branch below deployment; changes loop back to deployment. **Prototype only: no GitHub or hosting operations run.**

## GitHub connection

Connect the account, then create or select a repository. Check existing content before writing. Both successful paths lead to hosting. Source visibility remains separate from website visibility.

## Scope and behavior

The proposed Publish action builds a viewing copy, updates GitHub and deploys it. Editing the local notebook does not publish it.

**Integration decision:** external Git-connected hosts can deploy on pushes. The implementation must control which branch or event triggers deployment before promising “On Publish.”

GitHub Pages is supported today. Netlify, Cloudflare Pages and Vercel are proposed integrations. Account authorization and provider API details still need implementation.

## Building blocks

Actual Hypercanvas Chrome Button, Input, Select and Separator sources, SidePanel header/CSS, and the app’s compiled theme tokens. Local snapshots keep the notebook portable; provenance is stored with the component.

Brand marks and colors: [Simple Icons](https://simpleicons.org/). GitHub `#181717` · Netlify `#00C7B7` · Cloudflare Pages `#F38020` · Vercel `#000000`.

## GitHub Pages

Uses the connected GitHub account. Unpublished changes and failure recovery are shown separately.

**GitHub already connected**

No second authorization step. Continue to Pages settings.

**Deployment failed**

The existing website remains live. Keep the source connection and provider settings. Retry returns to deployment, not repository creation.

**Changes:** publish the next version through the same deployment path.

Connect provider → configure project → deploy → live. Unpublished changes and failure recovery are shown separately.

The existing website remains live. Keep the source connection and provider settings. Retry returns to deployment, not repository creation.

**Changes:** publish the next version through the same deployment path.

**Changes:** publish the next version through the same deployment path.

package-lock.json is a generation boundary, not a pretend handwritten lock. Shared dist build/upload is serialized; provider-side completion may continue independently.

## Recovery and cancellation

Failed first publish does not claim a live website. Failed update keeps the previous confirmed website. Cancelling stops local waiting; a remote job already started may finish. Retry keeps the selected destination and credentials/settings. Other provider progress survives tab changes.

Source push is a distinct stage. Failed push confirms no website publish. Cancel stops local waiting; check GitHub before retry. The success state still says Website: Not published. Repeat Publish updates needed source in progress without reopening first setup.

## Automatic publishing conflict

A push can trigger every attached host. Selected-provider-only publication requires all automatic triggers reviewed/disabled before dispatch. The conflict state blocks publishing and sends the user back to review. No backend or provider CLI was wired.

First push to an existing repository requires its automatic-publishing review. Selected-provider publication still requires every connected host trigger checked. Runtime source-push and website-publish examples are F05. This is a design contract, not executed remote behavior.
